FINAL HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, English — submission-ready):

"Increasing government education expenditure (as a share of GNI) is positively associated with subsequent per-capita GDP, and the estimated effect is larger and more robustly positive in Sub-Saharan Africa than in lower-middle-income (developing) countries. Specifically, a 1-percentage-point rise in education spending at a 2-year lag corresponds to roughly a +4.6 pp gain in annual per-capita GNI growth in Sub-Saharan Africa (interaction vs. developing countries significant, p≈0.02) and to about +6.9 to +7.5 pp of export-growth (an output proxy; p≈0.02–0.04 across specifications), whereas the corresponding association in lower-middle-income/developing countries is statistically indistinguishable from zero (−1.4 pp on per-capita GNI growth, p≈0.48) and imprecise on the export proxy. However, this between-group difference is statistically significant only on the direct per-capita-GDP measure and not on the balanced export-output comparison (interaction p≈0.3–0.8), and Sub-Saharan Africa's per-capita GDP series covers only 2011–2015, so the comparison is best interpreted as a directional, robustly positive SSA effect rather than a firmly established larger effect."

中文版：增加教育支出（占 GNI 比重）与随后的（约两年滞后）人均 GDP 呈正相关，且该效应在撒哈拉以南非洲比在发展中（中低收入）经济体更大、更稳健：SSA 组教育支出占比每提高 1 个百分点，人均 GNI 年增长率约 +4.6 个百分点（与 LMC 的组间差异交互项 p≈0.02，显著），出口增长代理 +6.9~+7.5 个百分点（p≈0.02–0.04）；而 LMC 组对应关联与零无显著差异（人均 GNI 增长 −1.4pp，p≈0.48；出口代理不精确）。但组间差异仅在直接人均 GDP 口径上显著、在平衡的出口产出比较中不显著（交互 p≈0.3–0.8），且 SSA 人均 GDP 仅覆盖 2011–2015，故结论宜视为“方向性、SSA 正向效应稳健”，而非确定性更强的组间差异声明。

payload.hypothesis: Increasing government education expenditure (% of GNI) is positively associated with subsequent (≈2-yr lagged) per-capita GDP, and the effect is larger and more robustly positive in Sub-Saharan Africa than in lower-middle-income/developing countries: in SSA a 1pp rise in education spending is associated with ≈+4.6pp per-capita GNI growth (interaction vs LMC p≈0.02) and ≈+6.9–7.5pp of export/output-proxy growth (p<0.05); in LMC the association is near zero and imprecise. The between-group difference is significant on the direct per-capita GDP measure but not on the balanced export-output comparison (interaction p≈0.3–0.8); SSA per-capita GDP covers only 2011–2015, so the comparison is directional and robustly positive for SSA rather than a firmly established larger effect.
payload.workflow: Wide-to-long reshape (group×year panel 1975–2015); missingness audit; descriptive + lead-lag correlation analysis (edu at lags 0–5 vs GNI level, ΔlogGNI, exports growth) per group; primary comparison = pooled balanced-window (1991–2015) regressions with SSA×edu interaction on exports-growth output proxy, plus direct Δlog(per-capita GNI) model; per-group time-series OLS (full & parsimonious, Newey-West HAC), AR(1) term for autoregression, time trend; robustness: lag sensitivity (L1–L3), no-trend, LMC 1975–2015 long window; diagnostics: Ljung-Box residual autocorrelation, residual AR(1), VIF. Associative/quasi-causal interpretation only (no instruments; 2 aggregate units).
